I have been working this land for 55 years. I know Quzhou's soil and seasons like I know my own hands. My wife and I only need so much grain — but I still farm all 5 mu properly, because that is what a farmer does. The wheat-maize rotation is what my father did and his father before him. I do not change what works.

My body is slower now. I rely on the village machine station to help me sow and harvest. But the decisions — when to water, how much fertilizer to put down — I make those myself.

For the **winter wheat**, I sow in early October after rotary tilling. I use the improved variety the county has been promoting — it yields well and I have seen it work on my land for years. I put down base fertilizer at sowing with phosphorus and potassium mixed in, then top-dress nitrogen at jointing. I water three times: once before winter sets in, once at jointing, once at heading. I spray for aphids and powdery mildew at the flag leaf stage — two passes. I have seen bad rust years and I do not skimp on this.

For the **summer maize**, I sow right after wheat harvest in June, no-till into the stubble — less work on my back and the soil holds moisture better. I use a hybrid seed, the same kind everyone in the village uses. I apply most of the nitrogen in two splits: base at sowing and topdress at big bell stage. Summer brings some rain, but I irrigate twice — once if it is dry at tasseling, once at grain fill if needed. One pesticide pass for stem borer and fall armyworm, which have been worse these past years.
